name: Oregon

notes: Gasoline pays a 40-cent-a-gallon state tax (since January 1, 2024), and 33 cities and counties add their own (Portland 10 cents, plus 3 cents in Multnomah County; Eugene 5 cents; ODOT table, read October 30, 2026); left out here.
Cigarettes pay $3.33 a pack (Department of Revenue); most other tobacco and vapor products 65% of the wholesale price (moist snuff by the ounce, cigars at most $1 each); left out here.
Liquor is sold through state-appointed stores at prices set by the Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission; beer and wine pay small per-gallon taxes; left out here.
Lodging pays a 1.5% state tax (2.75% from January 1, 2027) plus local lodging taxes (16% in all in Portland); not counted here.
Portland's clean energy surcharge (1% of large retailers' Portland sales) and the state's corporate activity tax are taxes on businesses, not on purchases; not counted here.
gaps: Oregon has no state or local general sales tax. Ashland's 5% tax on prepared food is counted in its restaurant rates, and Yachats' 5% would be where Yachats holds most of a census tract (it doesn't); Cannon Beach's reported 5% is noted. Lodging taxes (the state's 1.5%, rising to 2.75% on January 1, 2027, and local ones), local gas taxes and Portland's clean energy surcharge on large retailers are not counted.

4103050: Ashland's 5% food and beverage tax on prepared food and non-alcoholic drinks (Ashland Municipal Code 4.34.020) is counted in its restaurant rates; it was reported to expire in 2030 unless renewed (Ashland.news).
4184200: Yachats' 5% tax on prepared food and non-alcoholic drinks (City of Yachats, Ordinance 293) would be counted in its restaurant rates.
Yachats is less than half of each census tract it is in, so the figures here use the surrounding area's rates for its tract, not its own.
4110850: Cannon Beach's voters approved a 5% tax on prepared food in November 2021 (reported by OPB); it is in the city's code (chapter 3.30) and has been collected since 2022, per City of Wheeler materials citing Cannon Beach's finance office (March 2026). No city source giving the current rate was found, so it isn't counted here.
4140350: On November 3, 2026 La Grande voters decide on a 5-cent-a-gallon city gas tax (OPB); local gas taxes aren't counted here.
4103800: On November 3, 2026 Bandon voters decide on raising its lodging tax from 9.5% to 12% from January 1, 2027 (City of Bandon); lodging taxes aren't counted here.

programs: Urban renewal areas are mapped for Portland (with each area's status from Prosper Portland's latest report), Salem, Eugene, Springfield, Albany, Lebanon, Phoenix, Hermiston, Woodburn, Silverton, Turner and the Yamhill County cities (Carlton, Dayton, Dundee, Lafayette, McMinnville, Newberg). Albany's Central Albany Revitalization Area is reported to end with its current budget period, likely June 2027. Beaverton's and Bend's areas have no usable map, and the Oregon Main Street Network's communities have none.

warn.text: Bend draws many visitors (Mount Bachelor and the Deschutes River), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (4.5%) and its 79 lodging places (0.8 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs over the city as a whole, though 6 of its 20 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Florence draws many visitors (the Oregon Dunes and the coast), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (8.7%) and its 13 lodging places (1.5 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Jacksonville draws many visitors (its historic downtown and the Britt music festival), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: it has no seasonal homes, and its 8 lodging places (1.5 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's lodging cutoff. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Tillamook draws many visitors (the Tillamook Creamery and the coast), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (4.4%) and its 7 lodging places (1.1 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs over the city as a whole, though one of its 2 census tracts is flagged on its own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Pendleton's visitor flag rests on its hotels and motels (16 lodging places, 2.7 per 1,000 residents), many along Interstate 84 serving travelers passing through, though the Round-Up draws real crowds; read that flag with care.

John Day's flag as a visitor economy rests on its motels on the region's main highways (9 lodging places, 2.6 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers in a remote area more than tourists, so read that flag with care.

Burns' flag as a visitor economy rests on its motels on the region's main highways (7 lodging places, 2.3 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers in a remote area more than tourists, so read that flag with care.

Reedsport's visitor flag rests on its motels along US 101 (6 lodging places, 2.8 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through as well as visitors to the Oregon Dunes, so read that flag with care.

Gilliam County may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its motels along Interstate 84 at Arlington (6 lodging places, 3.0 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.

Sherman County may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its motels along Interstate 84 at Biggs Junction (8 lodging places, 4.1 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.

Ontario may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its hotels and motels along Interstate 84 (23 lodging places, 2.4 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.
